# Abstract {.unnumbered}

OpenPFC is a framework for solving partial differential equations on
structured, periodic, MPI-distributed grids, with CPU and GPU execution
paths that share the same physics. Its original target was the phase-field
crystal (PFC) model, but the architecture — a domain decomposition, a
distributed field, a pluggable spectral or finite-difference stack, and a
session that wires them from JSON — is not specific to PFC.

This report describes the sixteen applications shipped with OpenPFC 0.2:
tungsten, aluminum, cahn_hilliard, thin_film, surface_diffusion, kawahara,
ehd_film, higher_order_pfc, gradient_elasticity, heat3d, wave2d, allen_cahn,
kobayashi, alloy_dendrite_elastic, vlasov_maxwell, and inverse_homogenization
(an explicit catalog exception: PDE-constrained inverse design, not another
evolution demo). They span fourth-
through tenth-order spatial operators, conserved and non-conserved dynamics,
dispersive and dissipative behaviour, single-field and coupled multi-field
systems, a kinetic distribution on a phase-space grid, and both spectral
and finite-difference discretisations.

Four claims run through the report.

The first is that **high differential order is not high implementation
complexity in a spectral code**. A sixth-order elastohydrodynamic operator and
a fourth-order Cahn–Hilliard operator differ, in the source, by the polynomial
returned from one function. The equivalent real-space stencils would not be
comparable in effort. What high order does cost is stiffness, and the report
is explicit about how exponential time differencing absorbs it.

The second is that **the same application source runs on a laptop core and on
sixteen nodes of a GPU supercomputer**. That is a statement about the
runtime, not about every application. Chapter @sec-scalability reports
measured LUMI-G curves for two models out to 128 GCDs across 16 nodes:
tungsten strong scaling at 82% efficiency over a fourfold increase in ranks
at $1280^3$, and weak scaling at constant work per GCD ending on 8.59 billion
cells. The application sources are unchanged between the one-GCD and the
128-GCD runs. The chapter also compares the spectral and finite-difference
paths on the same equation, and is explicit that those measurements settle
cost per step and parallel efficiency, not time to solution, and that they
are equal-grid comparisons until the accuracy section converts them. The
kinetic application of @sec-vlasov is a different experiment: it strong-scales
on the host to the $N_{v_y}$ rank cap of its one-axis decomposition, and a
single MI250X GCD is 157 times a host core at $256^3$. It is not a 16-node
result.

The third is that **the two discretisations compose**. @sec-alloy-dendrite is
a thermo-solutal-elastic dendritic solidification model: a quantitative
dilute-alloy phase field with anti-trapping current, coupled to solute, to
temperature through latent heat, and to quasi-static elasticity through a
composition- and temperature-dependent eigenstrain whose energy feeds back
into the phase-field driving force. The local physics runs on high-order
finite differences with a halo exchange; elliptic mechanical equilibrium is
elsewhere in the same time step, solved spectrally on the same
decomposition. The coupling is real, signed and monotone: it retards the
tips, fattens them, and slides the operating point along the solvability
curve rather than changing the selection. At the conventional liquid-shear
regularisation $\mu_l/\mu_s = 0.05$ the tip slows by 17% and fattens by 11%,
while $\sigma^{*}$ moves 2.5%. That magnitude is a property of the
regularisation, not of the alloy: a 200-fold scan down to $\mu_l/\mu_s =
0.001$ falls ninefold, is still falling, and points at an inviscid limit of a
few per cent. With the temperature field on, the solutal and thermal
eigenstrains oppose each other and together store a third of what the
solutal misfit stores alone. The $512^3$ coupled run on 2048 ranks shows that
the machinery scales; it is too short to be a three-dimensional dendrite
result.

The fourth is that **the structured-grid abstraction is not confined to
ordinary physical-space fields**. @sec-vlasov evolves a distribution
$f_s(x,v_x,v_y)$ on a three-dimensional phase-space grid, deposits kinetic
moments, and couples them self-consistently to Maxwell's equations with the
Lorentz cross product intact. Landau damping, two-stream growth and the
Weibel instability each match a numerically solved dispersion relation to a
few parts in a thousand; Gauss's law is a charge-conservation diagnostic at
$10^{-14}$, not a constraint the scheme imposes. No other application in the
report has an unknown that does not live on the grid its fields live on.

None of the four claims is asserted without a number behind it. Where a
property has not been measured, the report says so — and where a number
depends on a parameter of the *method* rather than of the physics, as the
dendrite's magnitude does on the liquid-shear regularisation, the report
gives the scan rather than the digit.
